item.title: How Traditional Pithas Keep the Spirit of Magh Bihu Alive
item.description: As Magh Bihu celebrations draw near, households across Assam return to age-old culinary practices that reflect the state’s agrarian roots. Central to the festivities are traditional pithas: rice-based delicacies prepared using bora saul (sticky rice), black sesame, coconut and jaggery. Made over open fires or on iron pans, these seasonal dishes are inseparable from Uruka night feasts and Bihu gatherings, preserving flavours passed down through generations. item.title: Magh Bihu is Celebrated Out Loud but Cooked in Silence
item.description: Magh Bihu in Assam announces itself loudly with bonfires crackling in open fields, drums beating into the night, and laughter spilling over Uruka feasts. Yet behind this public celebration lies a quieter, tireless effort that rarely finds mention: the labour of women who prepare the food that defines the festival. item.title: Old Age Homes in Guwahati Keep Magh Bihu Alive in Their Own Way
item.description: On a cold Uruka evening in Guwahati, the courtyard of an old age home quietly comes alive. A kettle whistles near the kitchen, someone laughs while arranging firewood for the bonfire, and a faint smell of til pitha drifts through the corridor. Inside, elderly women who once cooked grand feasts for their own families now wait for the fire to be lit, hoping the warmth will make the festival feel a little more like home.
